sources.author: Carroll Quigley
sources.description: A wide-ranging historical synthesis of financial capitalism, imperial administration, international diplomacy, world wars and the Cold War. This supplied PDF is a retyped, annotated edition rather than a facsimile of the 1966 printing. Accounts distinguish Quigley’s interpretations from the later introduction and visible editorial insertions.
sources.pageConvention: All citations use 1-based pages of this 1,090-page PDF. These are not page numbers in the original Macmillan printing. January 1 and the first of a month are plotting anchors for dates whose day is not given.
sources.coverage: Selective, substantive extraction across the book’s institutional and political chapters, with emphasis on finance, empire and connections through the 1950s; selected 1960s developments extend the chronology. This is not an exhaustive index of every name, battle or theoretical passage. Selected institutional, financial and imperial passages in chapters 5–14 (PDF pages 47–229), with particular attention to banking mechanisms, Rhodes–Milner affiliations, constitutional reforms and the diplomatic origins of the First World War. Civilizational theory and passing references are not exhaustively indexed. Additional selected pages158–186 address foreign customs supervision, Japan’s political-economic organization and Chinese republican instability. Substantial reading of PDF pages 230–307, 399–417, and 449–454 within chapters 15–38, concentrating on the Versailles settlement, collective security, reparations, central-bank cooperation, stabilization and the 1931 crisis, British political institutions and labor, and the New Deal. This is a selective event-and-network digest, not an exhaustive transcription of every country chapter. PDF pages 472–792, chapters 39–65: Japanese and Italian aggression, British appeasement and institutional networks, European war, Allied strategy and postwar institutions, atomic diplomacy, and Cold War formation through 1950. The supplied PDF contains bracketed editorial interpolations; this digest does not attribute those additions to Quigley. Dates retain the precision supported by the supplied text, and known internal date inconsistencies are identified rather than silently repaired. Substantive reading of PDF pages 793–994, covering nuclear strategy, Korea, Eisenhower institutions, Soviet succession, Iran, Suez, Cuba, and Asian/African decolonization; selected late-book analysis pp 1011,1031–1034 and concluding 1963–1964 developments pp 1088–1090. Summaries exclude recognizable bracketed editorial interpolations. Citations use PDF page numbers, not printed-page labels.

events.description: Arthur Glazebrook established about a dozen Canadian Round Table units in 1911, working with Curtis, Kerr and Marris and supported by Milner. The groups supplied a local discussion network as well as material for the imperial journal. The Canadian units connect the 1909 visit to later Commonwealth conferences, institutes and the Glazebrook and Massey profiles.

events.name: Dawson takes the Times editorship
events.description: Geoffrey Dawson became editor of The Times in 1912 on George Buckle’s recommendation. His move from South African reporting to the London editorship gave Quigley’s network an influential press position, though a later proprietor dispute interrupted his tenure. This anchors Dawson’s press role before the Astor ownership transaction and later policy campaigns.

events.name: Lloyd George’s wartime coalition
events.description: Lloyd George’s wartime coalition brought Milner and several associates into government in 1916. Quigley portrays the change as an organized political maneuver that split the Liberals and gave the circle leverage over wartime management and the eventual settlement. The coalition opens the wartime-government thread linking Milner, Lloyd George, the cabinet secretariat and imperial consultation.

events.name: Imperial War Cabinet consultation
events.description: The Imperial War Cabinet brought Dominion representatives into wartime executive consultation in 1917. Its fourteen meetings and shared secretariat supplied a practical alternative to formal imperial federation while recognizing Britain and the Dominions as equal partners. This links wartime command to the constitutional development of Dominion equality and later peace-conference cooperation.

events.name: Smuts speaks of a British Commonwealth
events.description: At a parliamentary banquet on 15 May 1917, Smuts publicly used the expression British Commonwealth of Nations. Quigley argues that the speech helped popularize a particular idea of liberty under law, rather than simply inventing a new name for the empire. The speech connects Smuts’s prominence with the Commonwealth ideas promoted through consultation, scholarship and publicity.

events.name: Milner becomes Secretary of State for War
events.description: Milner became Secretary of State for War in April 1918 after involvement in the Allied command arrangements in France. The appointment formalized his role in military administration while his associates remained active around the wartime executive. This connects wartime executive participation to Milner’s subsequent work around peace and colonial policy.

events.name: Paris peace delegation and expert advisers
events.description: The British delegation at the Paris peace talks drew heavily on advisers whom Quigley connects to the Milner and Cecil circles. He examines how expert staffing and secretarial access shaped the negotiations without treating Lloyd George as an obedient instrument. The Paris network intersects the League debate, the founding of international-affairs institutes and subsequent German-policy arguments.

events.name: Milner states an equal-partnership principle
events.description: On 9 July 1919 Milner formally argued that the empire could continue only through absolute equality between Britain and the Dominions. Quigley connects this statement to the wartime consultation machinery and the 1917 imperial resolution. This gives a dated statement of the equality principle linking wartime institutions to Commonwealth constitutional development.

events.name: Irish armistice takes effect
events.description: The Irish armistice began on 11 July 1921, followed three days later by negotiations. Quigley traces Smuts’s mediation, his contribution to the king’s conciliatory speech and his attempts to persuade Irish leaders that Dominion status offered meaningful independence. The truce intersects Smuts’s Commonwealth argument, Curtis’s administrative career and Feetham’s later boundary commission.

events.name: Astor interests acquire The Times
events.description: The Astor brothers bought the Harmsworth interest in The Times in 1922, and Dawson returned as editor. Quigley argues that Brand engineered the transaction, securing ownership after the network’s editorial influence had proved vulnerable to a proprietor’s opposition. This connects business ownership, Dawson’s editorship, Brand’s career and the newspaper’s later foreign-policy role.

events.name: Egyptian independence declaration
events.description: The 1922 declaration concerning Egyptian independence appears as the outcome of Milner’s earlier personal negotiations. Quigley identifies Fiddes, Amery and Walrond as the officials around him, linking the episode to his Colonial Office team. This adds an Egyptian branch to the Commonwealth reform and colonial-administration threads.

events.name: Irish Boundary Commission chaired by Feetham
events.description: Richard Feetham chaired the Irish Boundary Commission in 1924–1925. Quigley identifies the appointment as a later international responsibility of an official whose legal and administrative experience began in Milner’s South African team. The commission connects the Irish treaty aftermath to Feetham’s wider legal-advisory career across the empire.

events.name: Milner dies
events.description: Milner died in May 1925 after decades of imperial administration and wartime service. Quigley treats the death as a leadership transition, tracing how associates continued through the Rhodes Trust, newspapers, Oxford appointments and Commonwealth work. The death separates the Milner-led period from the later Lothian, Astor and Brand-centered episodes.

events.name: Rhodes House opens
events.description: Rhodes House opened in Oxford and brought together scholarship administration, colonial-history resources and teaching space. Quigley notes that books moved from the Bodleian and the Beit professor received offices and a lecture room. The building connects the Rhodes Trust and Beit history chair to Oxford’s later international-affairs research role.

events.name: Unofficial Commonwealth relations conference
events.description: The first unofficial Commonwealth relations conference met in Toronto on 11–21 September 1933. Its delegates debated practical coordination among governments and institutions, recommending diplomatic access, staff training, inter-Dominion representation and cooperation with the United States. The conference joins international-affairs institutes, Pacific Relations contacts and practical Commonwealth consultation.

events.name: Peel Commission partition proposal
events.description: The Peel Commission recommended dividing Palestine into Jewish and Arab states with a neutral Holy Places enclave. Quigley follows the proposal’s British political reception and considers Coupland important in drafting it, while acknowledging uncertainty about internal deliberations. This connects imperial constitutional arguments, Coupland’s academic-policy role and the Palestine mandate controversy.

events.name: Hotel Majestic international-affairs meeting
events.description: British and American peace-conference experts met at the Hotel Majestic on 30 May 1919 to establish continuing international-affairs work. They agreed on an institute and a history of the conference, connecting temporary diplomatic expertise to permanent research institutions. The meeting links the Paris delegation to the RIIA, its first publication project and American institutional contacts.

events.name: History of the Peace Conference published
events.description: The six-volume History of the Peace Conference appeared between 1920 and 1924 under RIIA auspices, edited by Harold Temperley. It was an early product of the committee created by the 1919 experts’ meeting and financed initially by Thomas Lamont. The volumes show how the peace-conference organizing effort became a permanent institute’s publication program.

events.name: Chatham House acquired for institute
events.description: Colonel R. W. Leonard bought the house at 10 St James Square for the RIIA in 1923 after Curtis interested him in its work. Acceptance required an upkeep endowment and triggered a dispute over the institute’s financial commitments. This establishes the physical headquarters that later hosted conferences, study groups and wartime research.

events.name: Pacific Relations institute organized, in author’s account
events.description: Quigley dates the organization of the Institute of Pacific Relations to Atlantic City in September 1924. Its purpose was to study Pacific Basin problems through national units, creating a research and conference network alongside the international-affairs institutes. The institute creates a Pacific research branch connecting Commonwealth institutes to American and Asian delegates.

events.name: First listed IPR conference at Honolulu
events.description: Honolulu hosted the first IPR international conference listed by Quigley in 1925. The meetings brought national Pacific study organizations together, while repeated delegates and officers linked them to Commonwealth and international-affairs discussions. The conference sequence supplies intersections between Pacific affairs, institute officers and Commonwealth consultation.

events.name: Stevenson endowment supports Survey and chair
events.description: Daniel Stevenson’s 1925 endowment financed both the RIIA’s Survey of International Affairs and a University of London research chair. Arnold J. Toynbee held the professorship and editorship, joining academic work with the institute’s continuing review of world events. The endowment links philanthropy, Toynbee’s scholarly career and the institute’s annual research output.

events.name: Intellectual Cooperation institute transferred to League
events.description: France established the International Institute of Intellectual Cooperation and transferred it to the League of Nations in 1926. Zimmern became deputy director, connecting the Paris institution to the scholars and conference organizers appearing elsewhere in Quigley’s account. This connects League institutions, Murray and Zimmern to the International Studies Conference network.

events.name: Institute journal opens to public subscription
events.description: The RIIA journal opened to public subscription in January 1927 after previously circulating only to members. It extended access to discussions and published proceedings, eventually becoming known as International Affairs. The journal makes institute meetings and research available beyond a membership network, linking speakers to public readers.

events.name: Canadian and Australian institutes formed
events.description: International-affairs institutes appeared in Canada and Australia in 1927, the earliest Dominion branches in Quigley’s sequence. They built around existing Round Table participants while bringing additional members into a broader research and discussion organization. The institutes connect national profiles with the RIIA, IPR conferences and unofficial Commonwealth consultation.

events.name: Pacific Council organized
events.description: The Pacific Council was established in 1927 to maintain the IPR’s central organization between international meetings. Quigley describes a small, self-perpetuating body and uses its later roster to show links across national institutes. The council supplies the governing connection among national Pacific organizations and later institute tours.

events.name: Abe Bailey promises perpetual annual funding
events.description: In 1928 Abe Bailey promised the RIIA £5,000 a year in perpetuity, provided it never accepted members who were not British subjects. The gift made a long-term financial commitment explicit while placing a condition on membership. The endowment joins the South African, Round Table and RIIA threads through a recurring source of finance.

events.name: International Studies Conferences begin in Berlin
events.description: Zimmern began annual International Studies Conferences at Berlin in 1928 under the intellectual-cooperation institute. The system brought national perspectives on common international problems into organized discussion, supported by coordinating committees and several international institutions. The conferences link intellectual cooperation, academic chairs and the later Chatham House collective-security meeting.

events.name: RIIA acquires Wheeler-Bennett information services
events.description: The RIIA bought John Wheeler-Bennett’s international information services for £3,500 in 1930 and made them its Information Department. The acquisition brought an existing documentary operation into the institute rather than creating one from scratch. The acquisition connects institute publications, Wheeler-Bennett’s career and the documentary resources used in wartime research.

events.name: Rockefeller funds RIIA study groups
events.description: The Rockefeller Foundation granted the RIIA £8,000 annually for five years in 1932 to develop study-group research, renewing the support in 1937. The money funded a method of investigation through organized groups rather than only individual lectures. This explains how organized research became financially sustainable and connects foundation funding to published institute reports.

events.name: Chatham House collective-security conference
events.description: Chatham House hosted thirty-nine delegates from fourteen countries in 1935 to discuss collective security. Meston presided over the conference, Dulles chaired study meetings, and British participants submitted research on sanctions, opinion and policy. The conference links the RIIA, CFR, Geneva academic network and the contemporary debate over international enforcement.

events.name: Indian Institute of International Affairs established
events.description: The Indian Institute of International Affairs was established in 1936 at a meeting convened by Viceroy Willingdon. Quigley places its creation within the extension of international-affairs institutes to further Commonwealth territories. The institute intersects the Commonwealth organizational network and the profiles of Willingdon, Gwyer, Cecil and King-Hall.

events.name: Curtis and Macadam visit international institutes
events.description: Curtis and Chatham House secretary Ivison Macadam toured overseas institutes in 1938 and attended an IPR Pacific Council meeting at Princeton. Their itinerary connected Commonwealth organizations with American research and philanthropic institutions. The tour is an intersection connecting RIIA staff, Dominion institutes, the Pacific Council, CFR and philanthropy.

events.name: RIIA refugee study published
events.description: A Chatham House research program begun in 1937 produced a major refugee report edited by John Hope Simpson in 1939. Quigley situates it alongside appointments and conferences responding to Nazi persecution and the problem of stateless people. The report links institute research to refugee administration, Evian and the crises preceding the Second World War.

events.name: Foreign Research and Press Service formed
events.description: At the outbreak of war the RIIA moved research resources to Oxford and formed the Foreign Research and Press Service. Toynbee directed work answering government questions, preparing special studies and summarizing the foreign press, with Curtis supporting oversight. This connects Chatham House publications and Oxford facilities to the Foreign Office’s wartime research machinery.

events.name: Foreign Office takes over FRPS
events.description: The Foreign Office took over the Foreign Research and Press Service in April 1943, merging it with the Political Intelligence Department. Toynbee became director of the new Research Department and Zimmern deputy director, formalizing an existing wartime relationship. The merger completes the passage from independent institute research to formal wartime government service.

events.name: Curtis forms India constitutional study group
events.description: Curtis formed an unofficial London study circle in 1911 to examine how responsible government could be extended to India. Quigley traces its discussions to the later dyarchy proposal while cautioning that the original membership cannot be established with certainty. This connects Round Table constitutional research to the Montagu–Chelmsford reforms and the Government of India Act.

events.name: Montagu announces responsible-government policy
events.description: In August 1917 Montagu announced a policy of gradually developing responsible government in India within the empire. The pledge led to his Indian visit and the Montagu–Chelmsford Report, which became the basis of the subsequent constitutional bill. The pledge links earlier study-circle discussions to a public reform process and the 1919 legislation.

events.name: Government of India Act introduces dyarchy
events.description: The Government of India Act of 1919 introduced a new division of provincial responsibility and followed the Montagu–Chelmsford proposals. Quigley regards it as the period’s most important reform and examines both its public legislative path and its unofficial intellectual background. This is the legislative outcome connecting India policy declarations, dyarchy research and Selborne’s committee work.

events.name: Irwin announces Dominion-status goal and conference
events.description: On 31 October 1929 Viceroy Irwin announced Dominion status as India’s goal and a Round Table Conference to discuss constitutional reform. The declaration provoked opposition from British Liberal and Conservative leaders while opening a new negotiating framework. This intersects India constitutional reform, press decisions and the approaching three Round Table Conferences.

events.name: First Indian Round Table Conference
events.description: The first Indian Round Table Conference ran from November 1930 to January 1931, bringing British, princely-state and British Indian delegates into constitutional negotiations. The princes accepted federation, while Gandhi’s party refused to participate on the terms offered. This brings the India reform, princely-state and Commonwealth federation threads together in a specific negotiating session.

events.name: Second Indian Round Table Conference
events.description: The second Indian Round Table Conference met from September to December 1931 with broadly the same national delegations and thirty-one additional participants. Rushbrook Williams moved from advising the states group to representing the Maharaja of Nawanagar. The second session continues the constitutional negotiation and tracks the changing role of the Indian States adviser.

events.name: Third Indian Round Table Conference
events.description: The third Indian Round Table Conference met in November–December 1932 without Labour Party representatives. The British delegation shrank to twelve and included Hoare, Simon, Lothian and Irwin, now Halifax; Rushbrook Williams continued representing Indian States. The session joins the conference sequence to the committee and legislation that followed.

events.name: Hoare introduces Government of India Bill
events.description: Samuel Hoare introduced the Government of India Bill in the Commons on 6 February 1935. He defended the reforms as an extension of responsible government, while Churchill attacked the project and drew attention to the influence of a small group of advocates. This brings the conference and committee process into parliamentary legislation while showing differing political coalitions.

events.name: Halifax meets Hitler at Berchtesgaden
events.description: Halifax met Hitler at Berchtesgaden on 19 November 1937 to discuss European changes and a possible agreement among Britain, France, Germany and Italy. Quigley analyzes the German memorandum to explain what Berlin believed Britain was prepared to tolerate. The meeting connects Halifax’s personal diplomacy to appeasement policy and the subsequent Austrian and Czech crises.

events.name: Halifax replaces Eden as Foreign Secretary
events.description: Halifax replaced Anthony Eden as Foreign Secretary in February 1938 after disagreement over recognizing Italy’s conquest of Ethiopia. Quigley presents the appointment as the culmination of Halifax’s growing influence over policy while he held other cabinet offices. The office change connects the Berchtesgaden visit, cabinet disagreements and the later Munich diplomacy.

events.name: Lothian becomes ambassador to United States
events.description: Lothian became British ambassador to the United States at the beginning of the war in Quigley’s account. His long American acquaintance and Rhodes Scholarship contacts made the appointment part of the effort to secure closer cooperation and eventual American intervention. This launches the wartime Washington thread linking diplomatic, scholarship and Anglo-American relationships.

events.name: Lothian dies; Halifax chosen for Washington
events.description: Lothian’s death in December 1940 created a vacancy at an embassy considered crucial to Britain’s wartime survival. Halifax moved from the Foreign Office to Washington and retained membership of the War Cabinet, giving the post exceptional standing. This joins Lothian’s diplomacy to Halifax’s embassy and the wartime economic and information networks.

events.name: Brand begins wartime American service
events.description: Brand began American wartime service in March 1941, heading the British Food Mission and later representing the Treasury. Quigley follows him through May 1946, identifying overlapping supply responsibilities and the continuing Lazard connection behind his official work. Brand’s service intersects the finance, food-supply and diplomatic strands of Britain’s American wartime effort.

events.name: Isaiah Berlin joins Washington embassy
events.description: Isaiah Berlin became First Secretary at the British embassy in Washington in 1942 after work with Wheeler-Bennett in New York. Quigley connects this move to Berlin’s academic affiliations and his friendship with the Fishers. The appointment links All Souls and New College to information work, the Washington embassy and Berlin’s later scholarship.

events.name: Agenda journal founded for reconstruction
events.description: Agenda was founded at the end of 1942 as a quarterly devoted to postwar reconstruction. It operated under LSE auspices, with G. N. Clark as editor and editorial offices in Chatham House, connecting university research to the institute’s planning work. The journal connects wartime research with academic appointments and the effort to shape postwar policy.

events.name: Arthur Salter moves from shipping mission to UNRRA
events.description: Arthur Salter left the British Merchant Shipping Mission to become a Senior Deputy Director General of UNRRA in 1944. Quigley traces the move from wartime shipping coordination to international relief and later cabinet service. This connects the wartime shipping mission, international relief administration and Salter’s later domestic office.

events.name: Labour victory alters postwar network influence
events.description: Labour’s arrival in government in 1945 disrupted the circle’s ambitions for postwar reconstruction, according to Quigley. He argues that surviving positions in newspapers, Oxford, Chatham House and the Rhodes Trust no longer had the same unified purpose. This closes the wartime planning thread and opens the question of institutional continuity after a political transition.

events.name: Britain rejects Geneva Protocol
events.description: Austen Chamberlain rejected the Geneva Protocol at the League Council in March 1925. Quigley treats the decision as a decisive retreat from a stronger international-security framework, linking it to Dominion opposition and British defense-policy advice. This connects League enforcement arguments, Dominion consultation, Zimmern’s dissent and the subsequent Locarno agreements.

events.name: Locarno agreements reshape European guarantees
events.description: The Locarno agreements appeared to guarantee Germany’s borders with France and Belgium through five-power commitments. Quigley argues that their reciprocal terms and legal qualifications instead constrained French action on behalf of eastern allies and left Britain room to avoid enforcement. The pacts connect the rejected Geneva Protocol to the eastern-alliance and Rhineland strands of appeasement.

events.name: Anglo-German Naval Agreement
events.description: The Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 18 June 1935 accepted a German fleet up to 35 percent of Britain’s and potential submarine parity. Quigley criticizes the deal for weakening France’s strategic position while Germany rearmed. This intersects disarmament, Anglo-German accommodation and the pressure on France’s commitments in eastern Europe.

events.name: Germany remilitarizes Rhineland
events.description: Germany remilitarized the Rhineland in March 1936, and Britain did not enforce the earlier guarantees in the way Quigley believes was required. He regards this as the critical step allowing Hitler to strengthen his western position before moving east. The Rhineland episode links Locarno’s guarantees to the later Austrian, Czech and Polish crises.

events.name: Munich crisis and Czechoslovak settlement
events.description: The September 1938 Czech crisis ended in a settlement transferring territory to Germany after Chamberlain’s negotiations with Hitler. Quigley argues that diplomatic pressure and exaggerated public alarm helped obtain acquiescence while Czechoslovakia and the Soviet Union were excluded from decisive bargaining. This intersects diplomatic missions, newspaper arguments, military estimates and the Czech territorial timeline.

events.name: German occupation of Bohemia and Moravia
events.description: Germany’s occupation of Bohemia and Moravia in March 1939 changed the publicly advocated policy of the Milner circle, according to Quigley. The Round Table moved toward a grand alliance, while he argues Chamberlain’s circle remained more privately committed to accommodation. The occupation links the failure of the Czech settlement to alliance-building, Polish guarantees and national-service advocacy.

events.name: Britain guarantees Polish independence
events.description: On 31 March 1939 Chamberlain guaranteed Polish independence. Quigley emphasizes that the promise did not explicitly guarantee every existing border and criticizes the government for avoiding immediate financial and military arrangements that would give it practical force. The guarantee connects the post-Prague policy shift with alliance obligations and continuing arguments over territorial concession.

events.name: National Service Act follows conscription campaign
events.description: The 26 April 1939 national-service legislation followed a preparedness campaign associated with Amery, Grigg, Lothian and The Times. Quigley connects conscription advocacy to the circle’s changing response after Germany occupied the remaining Czech lands. This connects conscription advocacy, the post-Czech policy change and the approaching wartime mobilization.

relationships.label: Financed Peace Conference history

relationships.label: Donated Chatham House home
relationships.description: In 1923 Leonard purchased the building at 10 St James Square for the Institute, requiring an upkeep endowment yielding at least £10,000 a year.

relationships.label: Endowed Survey and research chair

relationships.description: Hope Simpson edited the Institute’s massive 1939 refugee report. Quigley explicitly says he was not a Milner Group member.

relationships.label: Study-group research grants

relationships.label: Partners and associates prominent in governance
relationships.description: Quigley says CFR officer and director lists were heavily populated by Morgan partners, employees and associates. This is the author’s interpretation of personnel overlap and influence, not a claim of corporate ownership.

relationships.label: Institutional influence described by Quigley
relationships.description: Quigley says the American Inquiry experts came largely from universities and institutions dominated by Morgan interests. This broad influence claim is attributed to the author, not converted into individual employment.

relationships.label: Executive organ of committee
relationships.description: Quigley describes the Paris institute as the executive organ of the international intellectual-cooperation committee.

relationships.label: Sponsored annual discussion conferences
relationships.description: Zimmern organized annual international discussion meetings under the Institute’s auspices beginning in 1928.

relationships.label: Nominated British coordinating committee members
relationships.description: RIIA was one of four bodies naming members of the British Coordinating Committee for International Studies, and could appoint three representatives. This does not identify RIIA and that committee as the same organization.

relationships.label: Oxford host and joint financier

relationships.label: Oxford host and joint financier

relationships.label: Joint financier

relationships.label: Department of the Foreign Office
relationships.description: The new Research Department belonged to the Foreign Office after the 1943 merger.

relationships.label: Founded under LSE auspices

relationships.label: Editorial offices at Chatham House

relationships.description: LSE was one of four bodies naming members of the British Coordinating Committee for International Studies. This is a procedural relationship, not evidence that all LSE staff belonged to the political network.

relationships.label: Opening speaker at 1935 conference

relationships.label: Australian memorandum coauthor

relationships.label: Regius Professor of Modern History

relationships.label: Wartime research based at Oxford
